summary: Cordyline australis is a widely branched tree endemic to New Zealand, recognised by its stout trunk and crowns of sword-shaped leaves. It is a light-demanding pioneer whose underground rhizomes can produce new growth after fire, while its scented flowers attract insects and its many small fruits are dispersed by birds. Māori traditionally cultivated and harvested it for carbohydrate-rich food and valued its strong, water-resistant leaf fibre for ropes, baskets and weaving.

summary: Nephrolepis cordifolia is a fern native across tropical and subtropical regions from India through Southeast Asia to Australia and the Pacific islands. It has been introduced widely beyond that range and has become invasive in some places, including Florida. It has erect, feather-divided fronds and an underground rhizome that forms several small tubers.

summary: Acacia cultriformis is a flowering shrub endemic to eastern Australia, where it grows in woodland on clay-loam or sandstone soils, often along rocky ridges. Its leathery grey-green phyllodes—the flattened leaf stalks that function as leaves—have a distinctive asymmetric triangular shape. From August to November in its natural range, the upper branches can carry prolific heads of bright golden flowers; the species is also widely cultivated and has naturalised on several continents.

details.use: eaten and used as an ingredient in some fritters

summary: Sida rhombifolia is a perennial or sometimes annual flowering plant native to the Old World tropics and subtropics. Its branched stems become woody near the base and carry diamond-shaped, partly toothed leaves, with small cream to orange-yellow flowers appearing throughout the year. Introduced widely elsewhere, it occupies roadsides, scrub, pasture and other disturbed ground. Its strong stem fibre was formerly exported from India and other places as “hemp” and used for cordage, sacks and brooms.

Crassula capitella is a small succulent native to southern Africa. Its narrow, pointed leaves are arranged in stacked rosettes and can change from light green to a strong red in sunlight. Erect or rambling stems may root wherever their joints touch the ground, allowing the plant to spread into mats. Toward a stem tip, the leaves become progressively smaller and merge into floral bracts around a long, pointed flower cluster.

Sciuro-hypnum plumosum is a leafy moss that forms dense, slightly glossy mats ranging from green and yellow-green to brownish. It grows beside lime-free streams and rivers, especially on silicate rock, but also on soil or wood, usually in moist or wet places above the average waterline. Its sporophytes are fairly common, with spores maturing from autumn through spring. The species is nearly cosmopolitan and occurs from lowlands to alpine elevations in parts of central Europe.

Stapelia gigantea is a clump-forming succulent native from the desert regions of north-eastern South Africa north to Malawi and Zambia. Its large, wrinkled, hairy flowers smell of carrion to attract the flies that pollinate them; their size and colour may strengthen the illusion of a carcass. The plant grows in arid sites on sand or rocky outcrops. When introduced to dry environments it can become invasive, although one report found it can also help certain native seedlings establish.

Atriplex tatarica is an annual native across parts of central and western Asia, Asia Minor, North Africa and south-eastern Europe. It tolerates wide nutrient and salinity gradients and can form large populations on highly saline coastal soils, as well as colonising roadsides, railways, dumps and other disturbed ground. The plant produces two distinct kinds of fruit, differing in size and colour, and its seed-bearing bracts can cling to vehicle tyres, helping it spread along roads.

Encephalartos altensteinii is a palm-like cycad endemic to South Africa, occurring from coastal scrub, rocky slopes and valley forests to isolated inland mountain sites. It can grow into a tall, sometimes branched plant with rigid leaflets and several greenish-yellow cones. Habitat destruction, collection and use in traditional medicine have led to its vulnerable listing. A specimen that reached Kew in 1775 is considered the world’s oldest potted plant.

Cakile edentula is a succulent annual or, in warmer climates, biennial plant native to North America. It occupies well-drained sand on ocean beaches, dunes and freshwater shores, usually above the reach of ordinary waves and tides. Its roots respond strongly to nearby competitors by growing more aggressively, but do not show the same response to related neighbours. The dry fruit does not split at maturity and is released at the end of the growing season.

summary: Ferocactus macrodiscus is a Mexican cactus found in high-elevation oak forest and grassland. Its broad, flattened globe develops 13 to 21 vertical ribs and bears curved yellow-to-red spines. From early spring into summer it produces conspicuous pink flowers whose roughly 200 tepals form a continuous spiral, grading from sepal-like structures outside to petal-like ones near the centre. Its name refers to the plant’s large, disc-shaped shoots.

Vicia disperma is a flowering member of the pea family. The supplied record places it in mainland Portugal, the Azores and Madeira and describes it as native in all three regions. Portuguese common names include ervilha-brava-miuda, ervilhaca-brava, ervilhaca-dos-relvados and orobo-amarelado.

Hesperantha coccinea is a semi-evergreen perennial native to southern Africa and Zimbabwe. Slender, lance-shaped leaves surround flower spikes carrying four to ten blooms in late summer and autumn. The flowers are usually bright red—the meaning of the epithet coccinea—but can occasionally be pink or white. Grown as an ornamental and for floristry, it is hardy to moderate frost, while colder regions grow it under glass.

Rubus sampaioanus is a flowering member of the rose family endemic to the Iberian Peninsula. The supplied record confirms its presence in mainland Portugal, where it is not protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation.

Coleonema pulchrum is an evergreen shrub in the citrus family, native to South Africa. It grows about 0.7–1.3 metres tall and is recorded there at elevations from 300 to 1,400 metres. Botanist William Jackson Hooker formally described the species in 1834.

Sedum hispanicum is a small annual stonecrop native from south-central and south-eastern Europe east to Iran and the Arabian Peninsula. Despite its scientific name, it is not native to Spain. Its branching stems carry short, rounded linear leaves and one-sided clusters of usually six-parted flowers, with white pointed petals marked by a purple midrib. It flowers from March to June and thrives in loose, well-drained rocky soil.

Carex otrubae is a flowering sedge found across Europe, Central Asia, western Siberia and Xinjiang in China. It grows mainly in lowland wetlands on heavy soils, including the margins of lakes, rivers and reservoirs and in coastal areas. The plant reaches roughly 40–70 centimetres, with narrow linear leaves and pale green or orange-brown utricles, the small sacs enclosing its fruits.

Sisyrinchium striatum is an evergreen perennial native to Argentina and Chile, where it grows in alpine grassland, open woodland and meadows. It forms a clump of grey-green, sword-shaped leaves around an upright stem. Clusters of cup-shaped creamy-white flowers, each with six petal-like tepals and a golden centre, bloom from May to June in the Northern Hemisphere.

Viburnum treleasei, the Azorean laurustinus, is a species endemic to the Azores. It grows on slopes in native forests with juniper, laurel, holly and heath, generally above 200 metres. The species occurs on eight of the archipelago’s nine islands.

Eruca vesicaria is a species native to Spain, Morocco and Algeria. Although some botanists have treated it as the same species as arugula, Eruca sativa, the supplied source describes differences in form and partial reproductive isolation between them. Plants of the World Online accepts the two as distinct species.

Musschia aurea is a flowering member of the bellflower family endemic to the Madeira Islands, including Madeira and the Desertas. It grows in exposed coastal habitats on sea cliffs and rocky offshore islets.
Dimorphotheca spectabilis is a plant in the genus Dimorphotheca. It is endemic to KwaZulu-Natal Province in South Africa.
Robinia viscosa, commonly called clammy locust within its native territory, is a medium-sized deciduous tree native to the south-eastern United States.
Oxalis caprina, known as goat’s-foot, is a short-stemmed South African member of the genus Oxalis. It produces bluish flowers.
